Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

vignette: Kofi had always been a man of calm and collected demeanor, but that all changed on the day his niece drowned in a flooded river. The memory of her small body being pulled from the water, the smell of damp earth and decay, still haunted him to this day. As a professor of environmental science, Kofi had spent years studying the effects of climate change, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma that would follow. At first, it was just the occasional flash of anxiety when he saw a large body of water or caught a whiff of something that reminded him of that day. But over time, these triggers began to take on a life of their own, sending his mind racing with worst-case scenarios and his body tense with anticipation. His students would often comment on how distant he seemed during lectures, unaware that Kofi's mind was elsewhere, preoccupied with the thought of danger lurking just beneath the surface. As the months went by, Kofi became increasingly convinced that his body was reacting to these triggers before he even had a chance to think. He would find himself scanning the room for potential threats, his heart racing in response to nothing more than a sudden noise or an unfamiliar smell. It was as if his mind had become hardwired to respond to danger, leaving him feeling perpetually on edge. This constant state of hypervigilance took a toll on Kofi's relationships and daily life. He began to avoid social gatherings and public events, fearing that he would be unable to cope with the crowds and noise. His colleagues noticed a change in his behavior, commenting on how withdrawn and isolated he seemed. But for Kofi, it was simply a matter of self-preservation – he couldn't shake the feeling that he was one misstep away from disaster. The stress of living in this state of perpetual threat began to wear Kofi down, making it impossible for him to relax even in the safety of his own home. He would lie awake at night, replaying worst-case scenarios in his mind and wondering what other dangers might be lurking just out of sight. It was as if he had become trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear, with no clear escape route. And yet, despite his best efforts to avoid them, the triggers kept coming – a glimpse of water on TV, the smell of damp earth outside his office window, a sudden noise that made him jump. Each time, Kofi's mind would snap back into high gear, racing with thoughts of danger and disaster. It was as if he had become stuck in this state of threat, unable to shake the feeling that he was always just one step away from catastrophe. It wasn't until Kofi found himself standing at the edge of a crowded lecture hall, his heart racing and his mind reeling with worst-case scenarios, that he realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this – trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and anxiety. With a deep breath, he turned and walked out of the room, knowing it was time to face his demons head-on.
